newsitem.title: FINLAND: LIPPONEN SEES SMALLER FINNISH 1997 BUDGET DEFICIT.
newsitem.headline: LIPPONEN SEES SMALLER FINNISH 1997 BUDGET DEFICIT.

text.p: Finnish Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen said on Thursday that the state's budget deficit would be smaller this year than the earlier projected 26 billion markka.
"This year, we will certainly achieve a better than projected result ... a smaller deficit," Lipponen told a briefing for journalists, outlining the coming autumn's political agenda.
"Total spending in the 1998 budget must be pushed down to the lower level proposed by the finance ministry," he said.

The finance ministry in July presented new savings to reduce total 1998 spending to some 188 billion markka, from 191 billion projected by the government in early June, cutting the 1998 deficit to 17 billion markka from an expected 21 billion.
The planned new savings could be implemented mainly by postponing outlays, Lipponen said.
"In the best of circumstances, the state finances can be balanced without any new major spending cut programmes, but not without some tightening adjusted to the cyclical situation," he said.
The Finnish economy was growing at a pace of 4-5 percent, Lipponen said.

"In conditions of strong growth we should get rid of the deficit as soon as possible and the budget should be brought into surplus," he said, but his prepared opening statement did not mention press reports of new finance ministry spending plans to balance the state budget already next year.
"Austere fiscal policy and moderate incomes policy will take Finland to a better future," Lipponen said, referring to this autumn's round of collective pay bargaining.
Together, the budget and the wage agreements should be targeted to boost employment, he said. Tax changes should curb the rise in labour costs and increase incentives to work.
The dimension of tax decisions would depend on the outcome of the pay talks, he said. He did not refer directly to any cuts.
